content.title: About
content.content: Mussels are marine bivalve mollusks that live in coastal waters of oceans and seas. They have tender flesh, a delicate sea flavor and a slightly sweet aroma. Mussels are usually eaten cooked – boiled, steamed or baked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mussels filter water, cleaning it of microscopic particles and bacteria.
There are over 3,000 species of mussels, but the blue and green mussel (Mytilus edulis) is the most common in cuisine.
Mussels can quickly repair damaged shells.
In ancient Roman cuisine mussels were a delicacy served with wine sauce.
Mussels can form massive beds called "mussel reefs" that stretch for kilometers.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Mussels provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent source of complete protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many seafoods, mussels contain very little fat, suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nerve function; mussels supply over 100 % of the daily value per 100 g.

items.title: Contain iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Mussels provide EPA and DHA, which promote heart and brain health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mussels, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Toxin contamination
items.content: Mussels can accumulate toxins (e.g., domoic acid) during harmful algal blooms; purchase only from reputable sources.

items.title: Foodborne infections
items.content: Raw or undercooked mussels may contain Vibrio bacteria, causing food poisoning.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Mussels are naturally high in sodium; people monitoring salt intake should consider this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mussels are typically cooked in boiling water or broth for 3–5 minutes until the shells open. They can be added to soups, paella, pasta, risotto, or served with a butter‑garlic‑wine sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh mussels are kept in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed container covered with a damp cloth, and used within 1–2 days. Frozen mussels should be stored at –18 °C and consumed within 3 months. Discard any mussels with shells that do not close after a gentle tap.
